prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology and molecular identity of glucagon-like peptide-1 that enabled incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six opening ballots place GLP-1 first, and I agree on the merits rather than because of that unanimity. The work runs from peptide biology (proglucagon processing, the active GLP-1(7-36) form, glucose-dependent insulin secretion in humans) to drugs whose effects are confirmed by large independent outcome trials in glycaemia, weight, cardiovascular and renal endpoints. It is original, mechanistically clear, mature and of very broad clinical consequence. A trio of Holst (human physiology and secretion), Drucker (receptor and gut-hormone biology and therapeutic concept) and Mojsov (identification and synthesis of the active peptide) is the most defensible basic-science allocation among the supplied names, and the prize can be framed around the discovery of the hormone's physiology and identity, which keeps it a discovery prize and not a product prize.
statement.case_against: The attribution is the real weakness. Priority among the early GLP-1 peptide-identification groups is contested, and the supplied credit list leaves out contributors such as Habener. Leaving out Knudsen means the prize honours the basic science but not the long-acting analogues that made the therapy work in practice, which some will see as an unfair omission. A GLP-1 prize also has a very high public profile, and I must make sure the committee judges it on scientific grounds and not on how visible the drugs are. I rely on recollection for parts of the priority history and cannot verify every detail from the supplied files.

responses.point: El-Manira supports Drucker, Holst and Mojsov but notes that Knudsen's drug-development contribution would be omitted by a three-person limit, and that priority among early GLP-1 contributors is contested.
responses.response: I agree that the omission is real, and I do not think we should dismiss it by calling her work merely industrial. Still, the Nobel criterion is a discovery, and the chain of discovery that links physiology to the hormone's identity is carried by the three. Knudsen's acylation strategy for half-life extension is an outstanding engineering advance, but it extends a mechanism already established by the others. I would keep her out of the preferred configuration, while recording that this is a judgement and that her case would deserve a serious hearing if the committee preferred a drug-development framing with a different trio.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranks CAR-T second but proposes only June and Sadelain, noting that Rosenberg's adoptive cell therapy work and the original CAR concept (Eshhar, Gross) complicate fair allocation.
responses.response: I share the concern about the credit gap. If CAR-T is the main alternative, the absence of the original chimeric receptor concept from our credit list makes any three-name configuration contestable, and I am less comfortable than the other members who include Rosenberg with the trio as supplied. I would accept June and Sadelain as the safer core, but I think that a prize built on the clinical translation while leaving out the originators is a weaker case than GLP-1, which is why I keep B045 as an alternative and not as a co-equal second part. The union limit of three people also prevents pairing it with GLP-1.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks BCL-2 fourth, citing the founding of the control of apoptosis in cancer and venetoclax, and Cory, Adams and Vaux as the central contributors.
responses.response: I ranked BCL-2 lower, at seventh, and I want to qualify that. The science is solid and venetoclax is a real clinical success. My hesitation is that apoptosis was recognised in 2002, that Korsmeyer and Tsujimoto are not in the supplied names, and that the four-name list shows how diffuse the credit is. Sandberg's point that Vaux's survival work and the Cory-Adams translocation work are distinct matters, but it makes me think a clean prize is hard to define. I would be willing to move it up if the committee can show a tidy three-person allocation, but I do not see one yet.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius places the unfolded protein response third and argues that Mori and Walter support a clean two-person prize, with other contributors arguably secondary.
responses.response: I agree that Mori and Walter are the cleanest attribution of any candidate on the shortlist, and that is a real virtue given how contested GLP-1 and CAR-T are. I did not rank B043 in my top five because I weigh clinical and physiological impact alongside mechanism, and the therapeutic translation of the UPR is still emerging. I do not think that is disqualifying for a basic-science prize, and I would not oppose it as a later or second prize, but I do not think it displaces GLP-1 this year.

uncertainties: How to weigh the contested early peptide-identification priority claims, including contributors not on the supplied credit list, against Mojsov's inclusion
Whether leaving out Knudsen is defensible if the committee frames the prize around the therapeutic outcome and not the discovery of the hormone's physiology
Whether the CAR-T credit gap (original chimeric receptor concept) can be resolved well enough to make B045 a credible alternative
Whether BCL-2 or the unfolded protein response merits a higher place once attribution is examined more closely
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for any shortlisted candidate. I note only that I worked with Paul Greengard (not a candidate) and have co-authored with committee colleague Thomas Perlmann, neither of which bears on the shortlisted names. No shared-institution tie is assumed.
